title: Residual Saturation under Pressure-Controlled Drainage
abstract: Here, pressure-controlled drainage is formulated as bond percolation with trapping on the pore-network graph, establishing a direct connection between percolation theory and pressure--saturation relations. In two dimensions, the deviation of the residual saturation from its non-vanishing thermodynamic limit obeys a finite-size scaling law with exponent $δ\approx 0.25$, independent of microscopic details of the lattice. In three dimensions, finite-size corrections decay more rapidly ($δ\approx 0.75$), while the asymptotic residual saturation remains finite and depends on coordination number. This extends the standard invasion-percolation picture beyond the breakthrough state, where the invading cluster is fractal and the invaded-phase saturation vanishes in the infinite-size limit.
summary: This paper models liquid drainage through porous media by comparing two theoretical frameworks: standard invasion percolation (IP) and pressure-controlled drainage modeled as bond percolation with trapping (BPT). The key finding is that BPT predicts a finite residual saturation in the infinite limit, unlike IP. The work uses scaling laws to characterize how these differences manifest across various dimensions.
main_problem: The study compares residual saturation under pressure-controlled drainage versus standard invasion percolation theory.
main_result: Pressure-controlled drainage leads to a finite, non-zero residual saturation in the infinite limit, contrasting with invasion percolation's prediction that the invaded phase saturation vanishes asymptotically.
method: The process is modeled using bond percolation with trapping (BPT) on a pore-network graph and analyzed by comparing its results against standard invasion percolation (IP).
model_or_system: The physical system is liquid invasion into porous media, modeled via a pore-network graph. The theory compares two drainage mechanisms: IP (local advancement) and BPT (pressure-controlled filling with trapping).
key_observables: Invasion-phase saturation ($S_I$), residual saturation ($S_r$), and finite-size scaling exponents ($\delta$).
important_parameters: Pore network size ($L$), dimensionality (2D vs 3D), and bond occupancy ($p$) related to capillary pressure.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on fitting power laws to determine asymptotic behavior, and pore-shape effects are noted as remaining important for quantitative comparison with experiments.
figures_summary: Figures compare BPT and IP saturation curves on lattices; one figure shows snapshots illustrating the difference in invaded regions; another details residual saturation scaling across different lattice sizes and dimensions.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical framework by formulating drainage as bond percolation with trapping, derives key results contrasting it with invasion percolation (especially regarding finite-size scaling), and analyzes dimensionality dependence through simulations on various lattices.
why_interesting: While focused on fluid dynamics in porous media, the rigorous application of percolation theory, fractal geometry, and finite-size scaling laws connects to critical phenomena studied extensively in statistical mechanics, which shares mathematical tools with quantum many-body systems.
